The Battery Factory Bottleneck Hiding in the Sewer Permit

Battery manufacturing is usually discussed through cathode chemistry, lithium supply, dry rooms, grid power, skilled labor, subsidies and vehicle demand. Those are the constraints investors and policymakers can see in factory announcements and earnings calls.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-02 · 15 min read

In brief

  • 0.425 MGD | HL-GA’s permitted non-process discharge cap in Georgia.
  • 2.6 MGD | De Soto’s wastewater capacity after its March 2026 expansion.
  • 6,240 m³/day | reclaimed-water plant planned for PowerCo’s Sagunto factory.
  • July 2025 | Panasonic began De Soto production before the wastewater expansion opened.
  • No named case yet proves wastewater caused a material battery-production delay.

The hidden gate appears after the water problem looks solved

Source document card / permit table

HL-GA signed pretreatment permit effluent limits

The HL-GA permit table makes the constraint visible: 0.425 MGD flow, TDS, conductivity, organics, nutrients, and metals limits for non-process discharge to North Bryan WRF.

Open source visual from Georgia Environmental Protection Division

Reuse: government public record; explicit image reuse license not stated · Attribution: Georgia EPD

The less visible constraint begins after a project has already financed the factory and installed its utility systems. A battery plant may secure water, add reverse osmosis, recycle part of its process stream and still face a second question: where do the concentrated salts, metals, organics, sludge, blowdown and segregated process liquids go?

That is the sharper version of the wastewater thesis. The issue is not that every gigafactory will run out of water, or that treatment technology is unavailable. The issue is that commercial ramp requires a documented receiving route for each residual stream and operating evidence that the actual discharge matches the permit and waste profile.

In practice, that means four things must line up: the public wastewater utility must accept the flow; the permit must authorize the chemistry; offsite facilities must accept the residuals that cannot enter the sewer; and the plant must produce credible monitoring data after startup. The gate is therefore sequential. It appears during commissioning and early ramp, after more visible construction risks have already been addressed.

Source document card / public response record

HL-GA response-to-comments offsite waste routes

The response record identifies offsite treatment, disposal, incineration, recycling, and hauling routes for battery-related residual streams.

Open source visual from Georgia Environmental Protection Division

Reuse: government public record; explicit image reuse license not stated · Attribution: Georgia EPD

Georgia shows what a permit-to-ramp system looks like

HL-GA Battery Company in Bryan County, Georgia, offers the clearest operating architecture in the current record. The Hyundai Motor Group and LG Energy Solution venture was designed as a 30 GWh battery-cell plant beside Hyundai’s vehicle complex.

Georgia’s signed pretreatment permit does not authorize an undifferentiated factory wastewater stream. It allows specified non-process flows: reverse-osmosis concentrate, non-contact cooling water, boiler blowdown and sanitary wastewater. The permit caps the combined discharge at 0.425 million gallons per day and sets daily maximums of 1,500 milligrams per liter for total dissolved solids and 2,400 microsiemens per centimeter for conductivity. It also requires frequent monitoring across metals, organics, nutrients, conventional pollutants and cyanide. (HL-GA pretreatment permit)

The response-to-comments record matters just as much as the permit table. Georgia EPD said the plant’s battery-process wastewater would be containerized and shipped offsite rather than discharged under the pretreatment permit. It also identified separate treatment, recycling, incineration and landfill routes for different battery-related wastes, plus a named hauler. (Georgia EPD response to comments)

The factory therefore depends on two linked systems. One is the public sewer route for authorized non-process wastewater. The other is a geographically distributed network of haulers, treatment facilities, recyclers, incinerators and landfills for the residuals excluded from that route.

The municipal layer adds another dependency. Bryan County’s North Bryan Water Reclamation Facility was permitted initially at 4 MGD, with expansion to 8 MGD. While that facility was being completed, Savannah conditionally offered temporary treatment capacity of up to 0.85 MGD for Hyundai-area flows. The agreement gave Savannah the right to increase rates or suspend service under specified noncompliance conditions. (Savannah sewer amendment)

This is what the constraint looks like in practice: flow limits, chemistry limits, a temporary municipal bridge, offsite waste profiles and continuing monitoring obligations. It is an enforceable operating system, not a sustainability slogan.

What the documents do not establish is equally important. No first-discharge characterization, discharge-monitoring series or schedule record in the current evidence shows that these conditions have delayed HL-GA production. The publicly quantified delay at the site was instead attributed to the loss of specialized installation workers after an immigration enforcement action. The wastewater mechanism is real; its effect on the production schedule remains unproved.

De Soto shows that infrastructure can remove the gate

De Soto, Kansas, is the strongest evidence that municipal infrastructure can absorb the prospective constraint before it becomes a lasting production bottleneck.

The City of De Soto’s current Panasonic project page lists a broad capital-improvement package of about $248.45 million. Its water and sewer components include $54.5 million for water treatment, $43.3 million for sewer treatment, $40 million for sewer-system expansion and $7.7 million for a water tower. The page also preserves a smaller 2023 civic breakdown, but those older figures should not be presented as the latest project estimates. (City of De Soto: Panasonic Electric Vehicle Battery Facil)

The city’s wastewater expansion doubled treatment capacity from 1.3 MGD to 2.6 MGD. Burns & McDonnell says the facility began operating in March 2026 after a progressive design-build process that overlapped engineering, permitting, procurement and construction. De Soto’s water-treatment work restored or expanded capacity to 8 MGD during 2025. (De Soto wastewater expansion)

The chronology complicates any claim that the new wastewater plant was a prerequisite for first production. Panasonic began mass production at De Soto in July 2025, roughly eight months before the expanded wastewater facility started operating. The expansion may have supported later ramp, redundancy, stricter nutrient requirements and municipal growth, but it was not required before the first commercial cells left the line.

That distinction is central. Water and sewer infrastructure can be expensive, schedule-linked and essential to full-scale operation without being the factor that determines the initial production date. De Soto converted the risk into a capital and project-delivery problem.

It also shows where the most visible spending moves. Money leaves the factory building and enters municipal water plants, wastewater facilities, sewer lines, storage, controls and long-term utility assets. The beneficiaries include engineering firms, construction managers, process-equipment suppliers and the municipal utility. But the same dollars should not be counted three times as developer expenditure, municipal asset value and contractor revenue.

BlueOval and Moses Lake are the clean contra-cases

The strongest challenge to an industry-wide wastewater bottleneck comes from projects where the planned load is small relative to available treatment capacity.

The U.S. Department of Energy’s 2023 environmental assessment for BlueOval’s Stanton, Tennessee, project estimated about 1.2 MGD of water demand and 0.33 MGD of wastewater for the 45 GWh battery plant. The megasite’s treatment system was designed for 5.1 MGD and included a 36-mile pipeline to the Mississippi River, along with partial water reuse.

For BlueOval’s Glendale, Kentucky, battery park, the same assessment estimated 2.4 MGD of water demand and 0.66 MGD of wastewater against 8.1 MGD of listed municipal treatment capacity. Those figures are dated design estimates, not current measured flows or legally allocated capacity. Even so, they indicate substantial nominal headroom. (BlueOval SK environmental assessment)

The project’s later problems emerged elsewhere. Ford and SK On moved to unwind their joint venture amid changes in demand, ownership and capital allocation. The water system remained part of the industrial package, but the strategic gate shifted to utilization and economics.

Moses Lake, Washington, points in the same direction. DOE estimated Group14’s proposed silicon-anode facility at about 170,000 gallons per day of water and roughly 100,000 gallons per day of wastewater, compared with 4.4 MGD of receiving capacity at the Dunes treatment plant. Some floor-cleaning wastewater would be hauled offsite, but the assessment did not present municipal capacity as the project’s dominant constraint.

Nearby, Sila began facility operations in September 2025 without a documented wastewater-caused delay. Its announcement described recipe refinement and initial production batches rather than full-scale output, so it is not a complete commercial-ramp proof. It is still a useful counterexample: at least one automotive-scale battery-material facility reached operations in the same municipal setting without a public wastewater crisis. (Sila Moses Lake)

Sagunto turns reclaimed water into a named procurement package

PowerCo’s Sagunto gigafactory in Spain shows how water scarcity can create a discrete industrial procurement category.

Lantania announced in April 2026 that it would build a reclaimed-water plant with capacity of 6,240 cubic meters per day. The system is intended to upgrade municipal wastewater effluent for industrial use at the gigafactory. The published scope includes clarification, filtration, disinfection and sludge handling, with completion scheduled for the second quarter of 2027. (Lantania Sagunto project)

This is concrete evidence of early commercialization: a named buyer, named contractor, defined capacity and delivery schedule. It is not yet evidence of delivered water, stable plant performance, recurring operations revenue or standardized contract terms.

The distinction matters because announced capacity often gets mistaken for market formation. Sagunto becomes a stronger commercialization case only after commissioning data establish output quality, availability, energy use, operating cost and integration with the battery plant’s cooling and utility systems.

Its schedule also creates a clean test. By June 30, 2027, Lantania, PowerCo or the relevant public authority should be able to show mechanical completion, commissioning or operational handover. A slip beyond that date would indicate that even a defined reclaimed-water package remains exposed to construction, permitting or interconnection risk.

Permits continue to matter after startup

Tesla’s Grünheide site and Northvolt Ett show why environmental approval is not the end of the wastewater story.

Brandenburg’s 2022 approval package for Tesla covered vehicle assembly, battery-cell production and surface-treatment activities. The state described a 536-page decision, more than 23,700 pages of submitted material, more than 400 ancillary provisions and 96 requirements related to water protection, wastewater, stormwater and treatment methods. The facility also includes onsite wastewater pretreatment. (Brandenburg permit summary)

A local utility later alleged that Tesla had repeatedly exceeded certain wastewater limits. Tesla disputed that position, and the original utility documentation, enforcement record and final disposition were not obtained. The episode should therefore be treated as an attributed allegation rather than a verified violation.

Northvolt’s own 2023 sustainability report provides firmer operating evidence. The company reported five environmental noncompliance cases, including excessive temperature and pH in treated wastewater at Northvolt Ett and excessive lithium concentration in treated process water at Northvolt Labs. The financial penalties were small relative to the factories, but the operating lesson is larger: actual discharge can diverge from design assumptions after production begins. (Northvolt 2023 sustainability report)

These cases support a narrow thesis. Wastewater is not necessarily the gate to first production, but it can remain a live qualification and compliance process during ramp and expansion.

The economic value sits in control points, not exotic technology

Most of the treatment technologies in these projects are established: chemical precipitation, clarification, biological treatment, membranes, filtration, disinfection, sludge dewatering and standard industrial controls.

The scarce commercial asset is more often the right to use a route. A municipal utility controls sewer access. A regulator defines the acceptable discharge envelope. An offsite treatment facility approves the waste profile. A laboratory validates the sample. A hauler connects the generator to the destination. An EPC coordinates design, permitting, procurement and commissioning against the factory schedule.

The clearest revenue today is one-time infrastructure and engineering work. De Soto’s water and wastewater projects and Sagunto’s reclaimed-water award are named transactions. The potential recurring revenue comes later through sampling, calibration, laboratory analysis, reporting, chemicals, maintenance, hauling, treatment and disposal.

But the evidence does not yet show durable pricing power. The named waste destinations in Georgia are approved or proposed routes, not disclosed revenue contracts. There are no public unit prices, reserved capacities, rejected loads or vendor backlogs. No software supplier has been shown to control the environmental-data workflow. No insurance policy or lender covenant demonstrates that wastewater risk receives separate financial pricing.

Value may therefore remain fragmented among incumbent utilities, competitive EPCs and pass-through service providers. Adoption can increase without producing a high-margin specialist market.

The closest historical analogue is semiconductor fabrication. Water-stressed fabs have built dedicated reclamation plants, raised recycling rates and integrated wastewater systems into site development. The similarity is the need for high-purity input water, segregated residual streams and large public-private infrastructure packages. The difference is that semiconductor utilities have had longer to standardize designs, operating procedures and vendor relationships. Battery factories are still in a more site-specific phase.

The claim that wastewater is the bottleneck does not survive intact

The adversarial case is strong.

Panasonic started production before De Soto’s expanded wastewater plant opened. BlueOval’s design documents show ample nominal capacity. Group14’s estimated wastewater load was small relative to the receiving plant. Sila reached operations without a documented wastewater delay. HL-GA’s visible delay came from specialized labor. BlueOval’s strategic disruption came from demand and ownership.

No named project in the current record has a primary or near-primary document showing that wastewater, reclaimed-water delivery, POTW acceptance or offsite residual disposal caused a material battery-production delay.

That does not make the permit architecture irrelevant. It changes the claim.

Wastewater is best understood as a late-commissioning qualification gate with asymmetric consequences. Most projects may engineer around it. A smaller number may discover during first discharge that actual chemistry, municipal allocation or residual acceptance differs from the planning model. The consequences can be severe at those sites, but the evidence does not support calling wastewater the dominant industry-wide constraint.

What to watch

  • By December 31, 2026: HL-GA confirms permitted discharge or publishes a commencement-of-discharge record.
  • By June 30, 2027: Sagunto’s 6,240 m³/day reclaimed-water plant reaches commissioning or handover.
  • By December 31, 2027: A primary record attributes a material battery-production delay specifically to wastewater or residual handling.
  • Through 2028: Two additional battery projects announce dedicated water or wastewater packages with capacity and delivery dates.
  • By December 31, 2029: Five operating sites complete a year without material wastewater-related restrictions or permit modifications.

The next battery-capacity announcement should therefore be read beside a second set of numbers: permitted discharge, receiving capacity, residual destinations and the date those routes become operational. Those numbers will not always determine the factory schedule. They reveal whether the water system is routine infrastructure, a costly commissioning task or the site-specific gate that appears after the rest of the factory is ready.
